key: Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help.
s: Midway through the opening surah, the praise of God turns into direct address; al-Tabari, on 1:5, reads the worship as humbling and abasing oneself before Him alone, preferring this to hope and fear because to the Arabs servitude is rooted in lowliness.
src: al-Tabari, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on 1:5, the Arabic text of the Tarteel QUL library via spa5k/tafsir_api, commit 9ae590a (2026)

opened.edition: Jāmiʿ al-bayān, the Tarteel QUL Arabic text via spa5k/tafsir_api commit 9ae590a (2026), editors’ footnotes removed
opened.locator: on 1:5 (packet.js quran 1 --verse 1.5), the opening gloss on iyyaka naʿbudu and the paragraph giving why he chose it

evidence.words: لك اللهم نَخشعُ ونَذِلُّ ونستكينُ، إقرارًا لك يا رَبنا بالرُّبوبية لا لغيرك … وإنما اخترنا البيان عن تأويله بأنه بمعنى نَخشع ونذلّ ونستكينُ، دون البيان عنه بأنه بمعنى نرجو ونَخاف- وإن كان الرّجاء والخوف لا يكونان إلا مع ذلة- لأنّ العبودية، عندَ جميع العرب أصلُها الذلّة
evidence.gloss: To Thee, O God, we humble ourselves, abase ourselves and submit, acknowledging Thy lordship and no other’s … We chose to explain it as humbling, abasing and submitting rather than as hoping and fearing (though hope and fear come only with abasement) because servitude, among all the Arabs, has abasement as its root.
